speaker: Speaker 1
words: The following is the interview of Minnie Badgett. The interview was taped June 20, 1975 by Dale Anderson at St. Mary's, Idaho. That way you can tell us how you want us to use the information on the tape. Okay, we've got a lot of questions we can answer and then you can just talk, okay? Okay. Your name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Minnie Badgett.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And your maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Scott.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Any nicknames? No. Is your real name Minnie or is it a short?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, that's my right name.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Date of birth?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I guess you'd call it Santa.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You're a real native.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was born where you go over to Santa, you know the crossroads, you know one goes over to Imagine Miller and Santa. Now not that house, it was another house but there's where I was born. Wow.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You were born at home then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, that's the way they used to do it. And actually, I don't know how in the world those people ever lived and existed. They'd be sick and everything, no. And take me now, I was premature, I weighed four pounds. And there was a nurse that lived somewhere that helped Mom all the way through. She was pretty sick with me, I guess. And then she took care of me. And I never lived.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, that's really amazing. Because I can, were there many premature children that lived?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, not to my knowledge. Of course, there are a few mothers that I've heard, been told about, that passed away when they were young. You know, for difficulties.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, let me just make sure I understand that I had done something wrong. Okay. Go ahead.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know, it was kind of, it was tough going on for them. It had to be. And they homesteaded, the homesteads all around the country here. When I was a kid, I remember we kids used to go and some of them would be, but the homesteads were made of logs. And they would hew and fit those logs together. And it's just amazing the work that was done now, that's all. And homesteads all, you know, just all, just all, all around the country, you know. Of course, they'd be no quite a ways apart, but they'd be the old roads, you'd have to go to them. And then now the way those old, now, you take one of these buildings, they'll collapse. They'll go down. But those old homesteads went from the bottom up. And the bottom logs are brought, see, there's no foundation, nothing to go around the ground. Unless they would have rock or something, you know, kind of, you know, underneath the bottom log. They were just built right on the ground. And then, you see, they decayed from the ground up. And you see they settled down, settled down, settled down. And the roof would have it, with maybe shakes, cedar shakes. And the roof would get holes in them. But the doggone thing stood for many, many years. It used to be interesting to go up them old homesteads. And then you see where they dug out their, had a little, where they had the garden place. And it's just, I guess, now and then, some of them would have, if they had a place where they had pasture or something, maybe they'd have a cow, but not too many of them. And maybe they'd have a horse. But, no, it was just darn tough going. Had to be. But they seemed, I guess, it was happy once you heard about it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. I do want some more information on your background. Your mother's family, your mother's maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Rothrock.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Rothlock?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Rothrock.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: R-O-T-H-R-O-C-K? Right. Her date of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, what was her date? I believe it was 1877, I believe.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Pendleman, Oregon. She was an old resident down there for both of us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And is she still living?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The date of her death?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And in what year was she married?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Her occupations or jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She's just a mother. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your father's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Frederick Scott.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you give me your mother's first name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Frances. Her second name was O'Nelia. Did you ever hear that name?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: O-M-E-L-I-A. O'Nelia. That's pretty.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know what I thought it was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I've heard some names similar, but not O'Nelia.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Her second name, Frances O'Nelia.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The date of your father's birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, that I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Do you know where he was born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was born in near Logan, Utah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The place of his death? Or date of death?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He passed away in, let me see, in 59. In March 59.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was your father older than your mother?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you know how many years older?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He must have been, oh, possibly five or six years older than her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So that could be just an estimate of his birth. I should know, but I don't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's okay. That just gives us an idea. And your father's occupation and jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he's a logger and farmer. Small farmer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sisters and brothers?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Let's see, we had five brothers and five sisters I had.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Do you want to give me their names?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, if you want them. Hazel, the oldest one. Brother George. Scott. Minnie Scott.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Addie Scott. Now you've got a lot of writing to do. Walter Scott. Pearl Scott. Well, I left one out there. Addie Scott was just after me. And I left her out. Well, we didn't write it down anyway. Addie Scott. And see, the last one was Pearl Scott then, wasn't it? Yeah. Edith Scott. Bill Scott.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Bill or Wade?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Bill, he told you. And Nina Scott. And twin brothers. One lived an hour and a half from the other one. I got you both. And they weren't named.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, okay. Okay. Now for your sisters. Why don't we just go through them and you can give me their married names. Hazel.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Hazel French.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Addie. Lincoln. Pearl.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Shamless. C-H-A-M-E-N-E-S-S.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Edith.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Smith.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And Nina.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Nina passed away when she was three years old.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, your husband's name.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Ralph Badgett.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Date of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Nine, um, 1898.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, Pamela in Oregon.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The date and place you were married.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We was married in Walla Walla.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the date?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: October the 7th, 1921.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the date of his death?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, the, um... October the 29th, 1961.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And his occupations and jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Farmer. Most of these people here was farmers and loggers. What is that? Couldn't do one, could do the other.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, children's names.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, Vernon. Vernon? Vernon Badgett.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And date and place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, he was born in Vimaida in 1922.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did, did you have your children at home or did you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was, Ike was born at home. In Vimaida. Ike? Well, we'll call him Vernon.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Vernon's new name, we'll call him Ike. And, uh, Virgil was born in Farmington, Washington at my mother's home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Farmington?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Farmington, Washington.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the year?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 1924. And Velma... was born in Sacred Heart Hospital in Spokane in 26. And that's all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, um, let's go through, you give me their occupations. Vernon?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he's a person at home, he helped with warfare, took up missionary work, was a missionary for, oh, about nine years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What church?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, the Baptist. Or the Undenominational is what they worked with, but they were Baptist.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And now he's down in, uh, they live down in Huntington Park, California now, and he is helping to purchase the age of us in the hospital, three hospitals down there. And Virgil, he's a loader here in St. Murray's. Okay. And Velma works at Sears Farm Store in Spokane. She's been there for over 20 years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What type of work does she do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She, uh, assistant manager.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's good. Would you like for me to move there? Is that your way? No. Oh, okay. Okay. Okay, your education.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Eighth grade. Oh, I went a couple years to high school, but couldn't make it. Well, it just didn't got him far to come from, he lied to down in St. Murray and worked for your board, and first one thing. Now, that was, um, it was very inconvenient. Oh. Yeah, same days. And the money situation wasn't good either.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. How'd you go to school before? Did you walk or what?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we lived right, not far from the school where they might have.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the only hardship was then getting into high school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. Well, it's just hard, and they just couldn't make it, that's all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, skills.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know about it. Oh, come on. Just housekeeping, I guess. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Jobs that you held.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I used to work in logging camps, and I worked in homes, and...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you do in those jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, waited tables, and then worked in homes, so I did whatever there was to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you did have some skills in that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. It don't take much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Your interests, talents, and hobbies.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it's just simply... Oh, I used to crochet and embroider, and I still do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever entered anything into a fair or won any awards?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, no. I've entered a few things, but never got anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you knit or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: All I knitting ever did was what some mama used to knit. I used to knit what she'd already started.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is she the one who taught you how to crochet?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Any clubs, groups, and societies?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I belong to the Grange, the Eagles, VFW, and War II. And then the... See, the Grange has a ladies' club, and the VFW has a ladies' club, and then there's another little club. I call it the Know Nothing Club. What is it? I signed up, and they called it the A&N, and so I called it the Know Nothing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh! What does the club do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, they just go and serve them a lunch, and they just sit around and talk. If they wanted to bring in embroidering, they'd do work, crocheting, or whatever they wanted to do. All those clubs, they do that sometimes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's more of a club just to get together?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's just to get together. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever won any awards or ribbons? No. Okay. That takes care of that. Now, I do have a list of questions here, and you can just kind of go off of that. I could go down it, or I can... I think, probably, if I just give you an idea of what's on here and what we'd like to know, then you could probably go from there. How about telling us a little bit about rural life and the advantages and disadvantages?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know. I think it was interesting. We lived down... well, have lived farther away from town, so now we're small. Then we lived not too far from the schoolhouse, Ardemida. Dad bought that place from the school, Ardemida. And, of course, now this was in my time. Now, go back earlier than my time, why the people got their mail from Santa. And he might have had no name. There was nothing up there excepting homesteaders. And the younger ones used to... Now, this comes from an older settler that told me. I used to ask questions, and I liked to know. I stayed with this lady one winter and helped with a chore. Her husband was away in the woods working, and she wanted someone to help. So he'd come up and wanted one of the brothers. Well, the brother was in the woods working himself. Well, I said, maybe I could help. Yeah, I could. So I had a cow and the elk, and there was a younger girl there. I had the horse to saddle up and get ready for her to go to school on. And some cattle to feed and some other horses to feed. And while I was there, I talked with her an awful lot because she was an older settler. Her folks was... Now, at the time, Ardemida was going to get its name. See, they wanted a post house there, and there were more people around there. And they wanted a post house, so the way they wanted to name it. Well, they figured the oldest settlers that were still living there, Ardemida, why they'd name him Ardemida. And so this lady, she was the East family. And so her name is East. And so E for East. MI for Miller was the next one. VA for Dawson. Oh, that's pretty neat. I thought it was interesting, though.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It really is. And...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, most everybody had horses. The horse to ride, the horses to drive, and the slidgings. The neighbors helped neighbors in them days. And now, like, I can remember my dad and then some of the others who lived with him. Now, they'd butcher beef or something. See, then they would divide it. And perhaps there'd be some family that didn't have too much food. Well, then they would... These men would... Whoever would butcher, one would butcher, and another one would butcher, and divide it. And then they would take meat from the raised gardens. They'd take vegetables and things to these people that didn't have very much to eat. And now, the clothing, the same way, leftover clothing and such, that's why they would help the bat too. Maybe some of them could sew, and even soap them. If the lady didn't have a sewing machine or she were sick or something. And now, when a tiny baby come along, why, neighbors took care of her. Which, I don't know, I just shudder every time I think of it. Because it was tough.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, you originally lived in Santa, right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, Emida.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, but you were born in Santa.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I was born at the crossroads going up there. But Emida had its name ahead of this. But I think that that would be called Santa. Because that would be where they would get their mail.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was it a little community where you were raised? Or were you just kind of out in the country?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, they would just that one house there. And the house sat down this way from where that house is now. Just down this way at these crossroads. And I don't know if there's any other, I don't think there's anyone close there, excepting who would live over at the Santa. But it didn't make any difference. Neighbors knew neighbors, and neighbors helped neighbors.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How far away were your nearest neighbors?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know. It must have been over at Santa. Or there might have been some other houses around there too at that time. That I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did your brothers and sisters be when you were children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we worked. The gardener age who worked in the garden and went out and helped other people sometimes after he was old enough to help. Oh, do harder than what's new.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you were younger, what did you do for recreation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we had, used to play ball. Girls and boys used to play together. Both their plays had a ball diamond we'd play on. And then we'd read, and then we'd fish. After we were older, why, girls would get on horses and we'd ride horses. Back. And then we'd have our parties at one house or the other and play games.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The baseball teams were mixed, males and females?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it just depended. But ordinarily it was because there'd be girls and boys, you know, at the homes where they would go. And they'd just go out in the yard and play. It wasn't no big, big place.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you noticed a change in the fishing since you've grown up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. We used to go out and fish anytime we wanted to. And then, you see, they have their laws now. And those things up there, well, you used to fish, and you see, sometimes they're restricted, no fishing, which is all right. It's a good thing. And then with the game and all, people used to go out, you know, if they wanted to hunt or something, they went out, they fished, they could hunt, they'd get their deer and bring it in. But there never used to be very many elk. Not close in anyway. And then later years, well, there's elk.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, was it easier to catch fish then, as far as, you know, just going out and the time spent?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I kind of think it was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I kind of had that impression, but I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You see, there was just families, you see, and the kids that wanted to go fish would go fish, you see. There weren't, you know, other, oh, maybe someone come of this and there's something and go fishing, but that would be all. And for that reason, you see, there would be more fish in the streams.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you or your sisters and brothers expected to go on to school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, really no. Because it just wasn't available.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What types of skills did your brothers and sisters have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, one sense of word, they should have gone busy with other things. There weren't many skills. It was help do what work there was to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did your brothers do? Did they get into logging or...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. They all logged.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And your sisters?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, housewives and baby tenders, I'd say.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We want you to talk about your courtship and your early married life. How long did you know your husband before you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, two years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did you meet him? Emida.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They moved from Rampanel in Oregon to Emida. And they knew our mother's people down there. In fact, Ralphie would chase around with some of them, those same age group. Had to be our mother's uncle's kids and aunts, however. They knew the family real well. And when they come out there to Emida, well, they kind of... Well, I don't know, there's some down that part, mama talking with them. Well, then it just kind of felt like they sort of knew her. But they had never met her, but they did know a lot of her, some of the people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were some of the things that you did when you were dating?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, they had dances around Emida and they'd have school programs. Had their Sunday school and church there on Sundays. Oh, they wasn't bringing me cars. Brother had a car and sometimes we would go out car riding. Didn't want to get too far from home. And the road's not that easy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were some of the reasons that you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't know, just wanted to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When did you expect to have a marriage?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I expected when I got.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, that takes care of that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think that some of the girls today would be more serious about their marriage. You'll really feel like they wanted to settle down and make a home. I think they'd be less divorces. But some of them are just not grown up enough. They just don't want to take responsibilities.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You were what, 20 or almost 20?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was almost, I'd say 19.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: About what age were most people getting married at that time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, around 18 to 20.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That sounds pretty good.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And some of them now, maybe 17 but not too many of them, most of them are 18. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you all talk about raising children before you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't know, just never gave it much of a thought.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have any certain number of children that you wanted to have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, never gave it much of a thought.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What affected the number of children that you did have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know, I enjoy them. They're all married. Grandkids.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many grandchildren do you have? Seven. Any great-grandchildren? One. Oh, really?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, one little boy. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did you get your knowledge about childbirth and child rearing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, just sort of come natural and from doctor books. Most every home had a doctor book. And that would have, oh, you know, tell what to do for different diseases and so on and so forth. It explained quite a lot about it. But, of course, taking them days, why, you come to St. Mary's or you go out the other way you could get out. Of course, there always was a way to get out, but not a good road to go on.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was there, there was a doctor in St. Mary's at that time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. Doctor in St. Mary's, as far back as I know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But where you lived, it wasn't a doctor. You would have to come to St. Mary's.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, or go out to Tico. You used to go to Tico quite a lot because there's a better road. Tico or Farmington. And it would take, oh, it would take several hours to go one way with the horses. But after I had cars, why, they don't take very long to go.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you see as the future for your children and your grandchildren?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know. At the present time, as soon as they're old enough to go to work, now Judy, that's my daughter's girl, now she went on to school and she's a technician. And she lives in Texas, she's down in Texas now is where she lives. And she's working with some doctors there with this technician work. And she likes it. She's getting along all right with it. And then Vernon, that's the older one, they have one boy and, of course, he's 15 and he's kind of that unsettled age. His mother and dad planned for him perhaps to go on to school, but now that's a question. You never know what they're going to do. And then I have a son living here in St. Mary's. And they have five youngsters. There's the older one, this is C. Kelvin will be, see he was born in, he was born in, 53 he was born. See that would make, he's 22 now. That's the older one. And these are running a truck for a coal company down here. Now those kids, when they were small, they'd grot and they'd pull weeds and then as older they'd mow yards and such of that. Those kids always wanted to work and earn money. And pretty good bunch of kids. Then after they grew up, my gosh, for a while, now Kelvin went over and worked in the sawmill at Plummer after he finished high school. Then he worked down here at the pie board mill for a while because he wanted to be closer home. And then, he's a little bit older this time then, and so he started working with a pole company here, and so they put him driving a truck. And so that's what he does. And then Dale, another boy, he worked with Mr. Titus here, helping him repair machine bins, such as that. And they patched tires for his car, a Buick Buick down here, was the first work they'd done after he was old enough to do that. Kelvin did and then he graduated from it. And Barry took over and he graduated from it. And Dale, then he graduated from it, is the way I put it. And then you see they had bigger other jobs to get more money. And after Dale was 18, he graduated from high school a year ago. And then he's been running a loader down here at the pole company, and Kelvin's been driving a truck. Now they sent him, he's gone to Orfino and he went down to Pasco and loaded poles. He's gone up to Montana, but they haven't sent him on any long, long trips yet. But they're getting, both boys are getting along good. And Barry, that's the second one, why he joined up with the Navy. So he's over in Japan.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, wow.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And, but he has written to me every week or 10 days since he's been gone.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's really amazing.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I sure appreciate it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's fantastic.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because, now I'll have to say it, whether I would like to or not, that mother is meaner than all get out to Jake's people. She won't have nothing to do with any of us. I go up there where they live anyway. Maybe she'll speak, maybe she don't. She's just an oddity. I pay no attention. That's all I do. Just come and go. And Barry, and the kids know it too. And of course she tries to keep the kids away from me, like mowing the yard and doing work. Why, they come to stay, come down. She wouldn't let them come. And so they just kind of grew, well, I'm going to say separate to quite an extent, although the kids do come to see me and such as that. But I wish it would be different, but I can't do a darn thing about it. She's just one of them people that's just selfish and jealous and just doesn't do anything to other husband people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you teach your children how to crochet and embroider?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I tried, but the girl wasn't interested.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you just try to teach them or?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I tried. I tried to get her to help. She worked a little bit on something, embroidering I was doing. And then when she was working pretty hard with her schoolwork too. And you see they rode the bus here to St. Mary's to high school, from Ida. And so you see their time was pretty well taken up too. But she learned to sew, and she liked to sew. And then after she finished high school, well, she wanted to go to Spokane and get her job and go to work. She said, she goes, she said, I'll work up to that month and come back. And her and another girl went up. And then she just, well, she'd come back home to visit, but she'd never come back home to stay anymore. Two years she's married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What's her married name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Jeans.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Jeans. J?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: J-E-A-N-E-S.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: N-E-S?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: N-E-S, yes. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she have any children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She had the one girl. Well, she had a girl and a boy, and the little boy died of leukemia when he was eight years old. So he hated that pretty bad too. He lived about ten months. Time he got doctored, he lived four, but he lived ten months. They gave him blood one time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It must have been hard on him.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. Well, those things are hard, you know. You try to do something and hope they are something, but then you see they're just, well, doctors do what they can. Ralph died with cancer also. He fell with cancer. And his dad died with cancer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Can you compare your life as a child with that of your children? How did it differ?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, as far as kids is concerned, I had more than I had. But I raised the kids in the 20s, and it was Depression time. It was kind of tough. But we raised a garden, milked cows, and the kids were little enough to help while they helped with the work that was to do there. So we made it okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did the Depression affect you? Were you able, because of that, to manage pretty well?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the Depression affect many people around this area?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think it did. Now, like you take with us, you take others. Now we're farmers. And, you know, you can raise some food and so on and so forth. Now, although there were some farmers that got discouraged, well, we were in debt. Others were in debt also. Well, now what we did, of course, Ralph was able-bodied and also his dad. And so they went out and they worked whatever they could get to do, maybe if they could log while they logged. And then they shut the logging down there just, boom, just all at once, both McGuldicks and Black Bulls. And then we went out with the thrashing machine and went out with the hay baler and earned money that way. And then we'd raise cattle. We'd have a few cattle to sell. We'd have pigs to sell. We'd have some chickens to sell. And we raised a garden. And, as I say, even them days, then we did help other people sometimes. And I will add to this now, and I'm kind of proud to say it, although I don't want to brag or say that other people didn't do, but now there was three places above us. Now, they had the same opportunity we had. They weren't as deep in debt as we were, that lost their farms to the mortgage companies. Well, what? Well, what we did now, they would, we'd just go and tell them ahead of time we didn't have the money to pay them their interest. And we'd pay as soon as we could. Well, then we'd wait and we'd save until we had the money and we'd pay it. And that way we never had any difficulties. Now, there was two other people I know that they had from mortgage companies and then they also had some, borrowed some money from some individuals. And so when they want their money, or from banks, not individuals, local banks, and then when they would want their money and go there, they'd go in a rage. We didn't do that. And some of the same people owned a mortgage on our place that owned one on another place. And so then people come in to collect, you know, see about how it's come along with their interest and their payment and so on and so forth. And them people, they just went in kind of a rage with them people. And this is the first time I'd ever met these people at all. I knew a load of money, but I didn't know who they were a darn thing. Rodney's dad was out with a hay baler down below in Midaways. Ike was a little kid. He was about four, I guess, this time. That's the older one. And so in a rage, why, they come there. And of course they was kind of shaky-like because they'd just come from this other place. And I told them her, her Ralph and Grandpa were working. And then I said, then you go down. I said, Ike knows where they are. And I said, you take him with you. And you go down there and you can talk to them. And then you come back and I'll have dinner ready for you when you come back. See, there's no place to eat there anyway. And oft times cook dinner for a lot of people. And so they, I don't know, they kind of hesitated a little bit one way or another. So I said, no, I said, that's what we'll do. I said, you go down. Ike go with you. He knows right where they are. And then I said, then you can see them. And when you people come back, I'll have dinner ready. So they went. There's the man and his wife and his mother, his mother-in-law that we owed the money to. And so they went. And when they come back, I had the table all set and their dinner ready for them. They was hungry too. And then they visited there with I and the kids for quite some time. I don't know, I think we give the kids each a quarter, I believe. And they know everything just fine. And then after that they come in. My heck, they just had a nice time. Some of them come in to visit when they come in. And no, we didn't have the money to pay them. And so, had to give it to them. And we never had no trouble that way.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What affected you more, the Depression or the war?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I didn't like either. But the war was really the hardest.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Which one?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: World War II. World War II. But, now Jake, the son that lives here, he was a World War II. The other boy didn't pass. So he didn't go. But Jake went. We called him Jake, named Virgil, but we always called him Jake. He was a little kid that's kind of funny. He'd be playing around out in the yard someplace. Well, Ike, the older boy, my folks used to come along. They lived out in Palmington for a while, and then they moved over to Sanders. Where they lived, Dad and I were logging. So they'd have Ike with them quite a lot. He'd see Dad, right? Ike M. Scott, Ike M. Scott, he'd say. And boy, he'd go with them. He'd be gone, oh, two, three weeks, maybe a month at a time. And then they'd bring him back. Maybe he'd stay, maybe he'd go home with them. And so, at any rate, my Jake was just a little toddler. So I'd go out, I'd miss him, play him out in the yard, and I'd call him. He'd say, I'm Jake, I'm Jake, I'm Jake. And so he'd let me know where he was. But Ralph and his dad used to be out working on the machine, you've seen me. And they both had the habit, now they'd be putting something together. Well, this Jake, this Jake, you know, meaning it would be all right. And so they'd take him with them sometimes, you know, they'd play around where they were working. And so then we got to call him Jake. And still do. He goes by the name of Jake. But that was interesting, raising the kids.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why don't you just describe kind of a typical day when you had the children here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What do you mean?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, just say it, at any age group, just kind of describe what the day might be like.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it was real interesting. The kids, oh, I don't know, do first one thing or another, play around, whatever they wanted to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you sew for them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not to, I sewed for my kids, yes. But the grandkids, I never sewed very much for them. Buy them things. Well, I see the professions over there, you know, and you can buy things for them. So that's what I would do. I bought a lot of different clothing and different things for the kids. And then when Judy, that's a girl, was in Spokane, of course her dad and mother both worked. But, oh, I don't know, I was visiting Ralph's folks down around Walla Walla. And this cousin, she had married again, and she had a good car, and he had a car. Well, they didn't want both cars, and so she said to me, she said, I'll sell you my car if you want it. And, of course, I had a car, and so I thought, well, now that would be nice, because, see, Judy was just ready, you know, to go to college, and she needed a car to drive to college. Dick had his car, Velma had her car, and I thought it would be nice to see her have a car, you see, to drive back and forth to college. She told me I'd have the car for $600, and pay when I wanted to, which I figured I'd pay if I took it. So, at any rate, I called up Spokane and talked with my daughter, and she said, no, she said, Judy's already got a car. And so then I didn't take that car for her. Well, then when Kelvin, of course the boys, you see, are beginning to work, one place or another, you see. Well, they needed transportation. And so I bought, Jake and Kelvin and I went to Spokane. Well, Kelvin made a few trips up there and kind of looking around himself. Jake, when he'd go up after machinery or some parts or something, he'd look around. So then Kelvin decided there's a car up there that he would like to have. I told him, you know, get something that was good, not get some old rattle trap. But they don't get a car. And with Barry, now this car that he got, I get $1,700 for it. And cash is what I paid so there was no payments to make. Well, at any rate, then Barry joins up with the Navy. He has a girlfriend here. She's a real sweet girl. I think a lot of her. And so then he used to come to me, and he'd go, and then when I said, what should I do? He said, should I sell the car or do you care if I let Shannon use it? Shannon and him finished high school, you see, graduated together. And then she was taking nurses training in Spokane. And she stayed at the Sherwood Hall up there. And there's no bus on Sunday, St. Mary's to Spokane. And so then when he was home, he stayed home at Santa. And then he had the car, you see, and he'd drive back and forth. And he'd pick her up and pick her back to Spokane and so on and so forth. And then he's going to be shipped down to San Diego. And I said, well, I think that Shannon could use the car. And I said, I think it would be nice to let her have it to use. So then he let her have the car then to drive back and forth. He was down in San Diego a while and back, and then he's down in San Diego again. And now he's over in Japan. And so then she has the car. But she's out of school for the present time. And she's working down near Mike's Drug. And her mother's working up here at the nursing home. But she has the car. I think it's real nice for her. She's not a runaround. Some kids had a car like that, how they would go. But she's not that type.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she come by to see you when she was here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. Her and I have each dinner. Well, even, I don't know, just after Barry. When he's been down to San Diego and when he's been in Seattle. When she'd come home on weekends. Now she'd drive the car up if she had the car. If she didn't have the car, I'd walk down and we'd eat dinner together. And now when she comes up and she picks me up and we eat dinner first one place and another. She don't have very much time to eat. And here, see, a week ago, Saturday, I thought I was going to surprise her. Sometimes I would cook and she'd come here to eat. And so I invited my sister to come over and I invited a couple other ladies to come and eat with us because I was cooking dinner and so might as well fix for a few more. And so then she said, I won't get off until 2 o'clock. And I said, that'll be just fine, I said. Come out and get your yard, that'll be just fine. And I just think I'm going to have dinner and go on the table. Well, pretty soon she called up and she said, well, Minnie, she said that Mama just called and she said she's going to come down and eat with us today from the nursing home. I said, that'll just be great. I said, you just tell your mother to stop by my place and you come up to my place and I'm going to have dinner on the table here. And so then her mother came down and we all ate dinner together. And sure enjoyed her. I don't know her mother too well, I know of her. But we had a nice time here, what little time it was. But I just had dinner right upon the table, see, and I just had to eat and go. Not very much time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you get together with your family a lot?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, not too much, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The ones that are at TAM?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not too much. Well, see, the kids are all working for one place or another. The girl, she's 17, she works down here at this auto freight, in the office there. And Sam, the younger boy, he'll be 16 in August. He's working down here at Charlie Upler's saw shop. He's repairing bikes and motorcycles and lawnmowers. All the darn kids are just natural mechanics. And so as soon as they're able, you see, they just... Of course, Jake took the boys to the woods with him and let him run the loaders and let him do different things. They never drove trucks, I don't think. In fact, he hadn't had any trucks after those kids were old enough to drive. But they just know. Just natural for them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you do for recreation, relaxation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, crochet some and embroider some maybe. I'll visit around one place or another. And go to these tubs, we have potluck dinners when we go there. One place or another. Oh, just kill time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was your recreation like earlier, right after you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there wasn't too much up there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I never did find out, when did you move from Imaida to St. Mary's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In 62.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you really haven't lived here that long?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's a long time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had to. And then we still had the farm up there to Imaida. We sold 1,400 acres. When Ralph began to get mad, we had timber. And there were three fires that started in the timber. Well, you know, pretty soon that would be destroyed and we didn't know what was going to happen. And we had this timber wallpaper, bought it from the Goldie Lumber Company. They'd log some off and then come along. This Mr. Lambers, well, how it come out here, what being nice to people did for us. Now, they was, they feared it was a man-set fire. But that we do not know. And when Goldie's had a camp that would be across the field from us, it weren't all possibly a quarter of a mile, maybe a mile from our house. And so Ralph and Gramps saw the fire. They were out in the field, so they went over there to that fire. I was fighting on it. I think that Ralph went and walked on into camp, which wasn't too far and reported it. And it was right in the hot summertime. And so then they had to get men to come and fight that fire. And Ralph and Gramps were right there on the job. And then they stayed there all night to save a railroad bridge. And they saved that bridge from burning by staying there. And some men, you know, all worked so long and tail with it. They got lots of money. They're a company. They got lots of money and, boy, they would go, you know. And so at any rate, why then they did know that Ralph and his dad saved that bridge by staying there all night. I knew they were out fighting fire, but I didn't know where, what, or when. And the kids were small, and no need for me to go out to try to find them. Because they could come home better than I could ever find them. And then they brought food to them while they were there. I don't know how someone, a man, reported it and told him that they were there at the bridge or something. But I don't know. Maybe they come and found them there. At any rate, they brought food to them there because they didn't fear if they left, why, the bridge would burn. And so then it went on for, oh, every time they'd see Ralph or Gramps out, you know, near the road or anything, why, this Mr. Lammers would stop and talk with them and so on and so forth. And it went on for some time, and they put in some logs for him as well. And then they, he would stop then, and they had shut their camp down there at this time, you see. Well, it's beginning this real tough time, and there's no work, there's no markets, there wasn't anything. So Mr. Lammers would come along and he would stop and talk to them, and I want to sell you 40 acres, joining you. Well, then we'd take that 40 acres, and then we'd manage some of the sawmills around, you see, and we'd put in timber to pay for it, and he sold it very, very cheap.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How much did the sell for?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Part of it we only paid two and a half an acre, and that was some timber that had never been logged.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You mean 215 acres?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, $2, that's right, $2.50 an acre. And then some of it paid around, I think around $9, much paid for any of it. Now some of it had been, some logs taken out of it, some of it never been touched. We bought 1,400 acres of it that way.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wow.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And it was all joining, and it was darn good timber. Well, but then there's three fires that started in it. Well, we fairs man-made, because someone would come along, there was a jealousy. And, well, ain't you going to put some logs in? We need work. Put some logs in. I thought you was going to log in one job. Well, we couldn't put men there in the woods to work, and then Ralph weren't able to go in the woods and watch. Now ahead of that we had put some men in the woods that we could trust, let them go and take some of the timber out. But it comes a little bit beyond that. And so then there was three fires. They got a hold of them before they were very big, because, see, the foresters would see. And so they sent their men down to fight and put them out. And so then just decided, well, maybe better sell it and save difficulties. And so then we sold it, sold it, 1,400 acres. We didn't get too much out of it, because it wasn't, well, just wasn't much price at that time, you see. Now and later if I'd kept that thing, it would have been worth $100,000. I could talk.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where is it? Is it out by a mine, or is it close?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's out of Umida. You see, it joined our farm ground, and then we had some timber on part of our stuff too. We hadn't cleared it all up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When did you sell it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I sold the place in 66, when I could get on Social Security. But I would go up there. That was hard. You see, I'd have to go up there, and I'd have to get someone, you see, to fix the fences. I'd go around the fences, and then I'd spray the thistles, get someone to do that. And cattle break in. See, we'd put it in the soil bank or pastured. Now this is even part of the meadow ground that's pastured. And so it just got, it was a hard job. And fences, you know, they go down more and more and more and more all the time. And now the inside fences, I let them go to heck. I never tried to, well, it's just too darn hard to get labor to do it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did you own your farm?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, Badger's come there in 1919. I bought the first place, and then we bought, you see, this other ground different years, you see, as time went on. And two of these places that we bought were places that, say, a few years earlier than that had gone back to mortgage companies. And they were the mortgage companies that we bought them from, two of them. But, and that was some years after the people had given them up. Of course, the first thing they'd do when they'd go and take the place back was come down to Badger's and see if they wouldn't buy it. But, well, we could have it. We didn't want to do that. Because the friends and neighbors, you know, why it just wouldn't, so we wouldn't do that. And the one place why it rented for three or four years, and then we rented it, and then bought it later. That worked out better because, and that way we're friends.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I just can't get over buying land for $2.50 or $9 an acre.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yep, we paid $2.50 an acre for it. Well, now, it was worth more money than that. And he would have never sold it to anyone else for that price. Well, they said they wouldn't. But they was moving their logging out, and that bunch of timber was all that McGoldrick's had left in there that, you know, adjoining. They had more, you see, but that was kind of but sell. And they did that. Well, I told Ralph I was going to make him a cattle ranch. And that was the reason that he sold that, was just because it saved that bridge. And they appreciated it. Wow. But, well, as you know how some people, others went up there and tried to buy part of that, and they wouldn't sell to anyone. They wouldn't sell it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's really interesting.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But then we got it, but if we were to cap it. And then, now, Jake and Rose, we still had that timber. And Jake was working up on Charlotte Creek. And they were living here in St. Murray's, and he was driving back and forth. Well, his little house was for sale. It was a nice little house. And while he seemingly never had any money, although he worked hard and earned good money. But, so Ralph asked him, him and her, if they wouldn't like to live at his. Why didn't we buy that place for them?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, fine.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So, they didn't have any kids at this time. So we bought this place, little house for them. They didn't pay for it, given the deed and title to it. And they lived up there for, oh, there's there, oh, between two and three years they lived there. And then they had two little boys at this time. And then she's going to come to St. Murray's and get away from the goddamn Badgets. And so Mr. Blodgett, that's the man who owned the store then, he told us about it. She went down to the store, one of them mouthy ones. And Blodgett asked her what she was going to do with the two little Badgets. Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha! Oh, it was funny. Got the biggest kick out of him. But now, what he would do, she would come down there in the store and he just liked to ag her and get her, you know, custom Badgets. Well, we were close friends of Blodgett's and banged forth and everything. He had the store there. And he just could get the kick out of it. And I thought that was pretty good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's beautiful.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I thought that was real cute.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Who fixed up the house for you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I've had different ones come. Now Mr. Fly, the man that lives over here, and a nephew that lives in Spokane, come down and really did the work. Lowering the ceilings and putting this paneling in. Oh, did a lot of work here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What made you decide to move to St. Mary's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I didn't want to live up there, on the ranch by myself. And Grandpa had cancer. He weren't well either. And he'd be in and out of the hospital some. And so then we rented here at first. And to be out, Daniel was out before he passed away. We, Daniel, rented about, oh, six weeks before he passed away. And then we started looking around to buy something. And then this was up for sale, and I grabbed it. After Ralph passed away. You know, all these funny things. And then when I started telling you about this tree, why, when I was a kid, we used to come down, used to bring beef or pigs or chickens, or come to St. Mary's. There's a crooked, narrow road. This horse stays. And so Dad used to bring, when he'd come down, he'd bring home maybe two of us kids with him, or three of us. However, we'd take our turns coming to St. Mary's. Boy, that was a treat! To drive down, and he'd put the horses and livers stable here, and take it, and we'd go to a restaurant and eat. And boy, you know, that was, that was something. Our Dad was very, very good to us kids. And so then we'd come down, and so he was across the canyon, and this tree had a tongue through it. Right through that tree.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you mean?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, what happened, this was in stagecoach days, and then the freight, and you see, beef freight, you see, with four or six horses, however many horses they needed, you see, to pull these wagons. The stagecoach carried the mail, and some things too, they'd put four horses on that. And they raked this with a freight wagon. And they would come down, they had all, which would have well-trained young horses on these rigs, because, see, it was a hard trip. They'd really go, they'd go up here to what they called the halfway house, and they'd change the horses. Put on more, and away they'd go, see, they'd just make the horses go as fast as they could really, you know, take the trip, and then come back and change horses again on the way back. And so at any rate, they was coming from up toward Clarkie, and of course they needed young horses too, that were tough to take the trip. And so they were coming down from up there, and then they used to be mining up in, up at Tyson Creek, mines up in there, and had quite a lot of big machinery up in there. That would be in the 1900s. And so at any rate, I don't know the year, but it'd be some in the early days. And this story was told to me. And so these men were coming down, and they had either four or six horses on this freight wagon, coming down a hill, and they had kags or something in there that rattled in the back of this rig, and it scared the horses, and they started to run. And so the man couldn't hold them. And they had going around crooked road turns, so on and so forth, and there was a turn they would have to come to, you see, in which he knew. He said, jump, jump, jump, the driver said, this other man. And so this man jumped out from the wagon, and then this other man jumped. They're driving the horses, and he says, go you horses, go. I can buy more horses, but no more old Joe. And the horses missed the turn, you see, because they go this way, they missed the turn. And so the horses, and down in the brush and small trees and all, but see, they were going at a high rate of speed, and the tongue went through, see, one horse on one side, pretty near on the other, and the tongue went through the tree. And I was told, and I do believe this to be right, that the horses were all killed. And it just sounds reasonable, although some tells me that the horses weren't killed. But the man that told this story to me, the horses were killed, which you can almost believe. And that tongue was in that tree. Well, that tree grew up. It didn't kill the tree. The tree grew up with that tongue in it. And so when we come to St. Mary's, we like to, you know, look across, we see that tongue way up in the tree.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is it still there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And not now. And so anyway, it went on then for several years, and it's only been, it hadn't been too many years since that that tree was cut down. That's why I was going to look and show you a picture, because I've got a clipping of it here somewhere. And they cut the tree down and took it down and put a museum in Boise. And then I've been told since that they took it to New York, and a museum there, with the tongue in the tree. But what I was told that they cut the tongue partly off. It's still through the tree, you see, but it's not the big long tongue that was that we used to see. And that tree grew.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's too bad they didn't leave it in Idaho. I think that's where it belongs.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, but that's the story I got. It might still be down here in Boise. Now, I'm not a saying, but I've been told that they did ship it, that they did ship the tree to a museum in New York City. Now, whether that's right or not, I don't know. If you ever go down to Boise, well, you go to the museum, then you see where it's there or not. And it might possibly be there. No, it's... Oh, there's just a lot of things. And now, but I'm going to tell you now while you're here, where that you can get a lot more information that's already written down. That'll be of our country here. That'll be from Wallace, Kellogg, and all down the way here, which there used to be mines there. And you will hold your breath when you read some of those stories.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, well, what we're doing is we're getting women's lives. We are going to go up to the Wallace-Kellogg area sometime next month, and we'll be interviewing women up there. We feel like there's a lot of history that's written down, but a lot of it's basically about the men. And so we're interested in finding out what the women did. And we think that that's important, and we think that a woman's viewpoint is important, and that we just hate for it to get lost.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's right. Well, now there's a place over here in Cardinal Lane. I had bought some of the books. One was Steamboat on the River. I had that book. And then I had other books that I had bought. You see, that would be the early day history. And that gives the names, and that gives the dates of happenings. And over at Cardinal Lane is where I bought some of the books, and I had them here. And then Morales folks will come. Now some of them come from North Carolina, and some of them come from Iowa to come here to visit me. Some of them from around Pendleton, Oregon, Walla Walla, that part comes. And then they've been all interested with those books. Well, Grandpa's brother was here last fall, and his wife. They go down to San Anne and spend the winter, and then they go back to Corning, Iowa, and spend the summer. They have a son there that they have a big farm there, and the son lives on the farm, and he's back there to help him. And they were here last fall. They stayed here for four or five days. And then, I don't know, I asked him if he'd like to read anything interesting. And so he read some of them books while he was here, and then I let him have the rest of them. And then, you see, he would take them home because he were interested, and then the people there in Iowa would be too. And that gives the dates, and that gives the names.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you traveled much outside of Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not too much. Ike and I, we lived in Kansas City, and we went to visit them there a few days, Ralph and Gramps and I. Then they lived at Lemon, South Dakota. That's—they moved there before Ralph passed away, but he never went there to visit them. And so I made trips there sometimes to visit them while they were there. And then Ralph and I took a trip down. They lived in Huntington Park. That's all 15 years or more ago before they started this other chasing around, one place or another. Where is Huntington Park?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Huh? What state is Huntington Park in?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: California. It's a sub of L.A. Oh. And we went down there and visited both of them, Ralph and I.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you think of L.A.?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I like it. It's nice. There's many interesting things. And then Ike and Audrey are back there again now, they live. And so I'm going down to visit them before too long.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you ever want to live there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think so. No, I like the smaller towns better, I think.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see. Oh, yeah, you were talking about having a garden. Did you can and freeze things?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we never had no freezers, and we had no refrigerators. No, we'd raise our vegetables, and we had cellars, and we'd put them down in the cellar underneath the house. Some cellars were built under the house, and some were built no out, but that's the way people kept their vegetables.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you can?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I can fruit and something, but I didn't can vegetables. I didn't have time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you dry anything? No. Have you ever made soap?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you still do it? No. When did you make soap?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't know. It's a fairly minor. Mama used to make soap, and then some of the older ladies did, and then they'd buy some soap too. And then I made, used to make soap. Ralph's mother used to like that soap, and so she used to make soap. I made it a time or two after she passed away, in 25. I wasn't, oh, I'd be doing other things. That's the job, making that soap.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was it, did you buy the lye, or did you make your own lye?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Bought the lye. I wouldn't know even how to make it now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: My husband and I had made some soap, and I thought it was fairly simple to do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I'll tell you the way that, well, there's a simple way to make it, and then there's another way. Now, we used to put it in some big container, and then we'd stir and stir and stir and stir it. Did you make it that way, or the?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We'd just heat the fats and have the lye, a lye solution that was warm, and just pour it in together. We'd probably have to stir it 30, 45 minutes, and that was all. Of course, we only made a small batch, just you know, maybe that big.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, see, that would seem cool, and so you see that would be all right. But then take more of it, and make, you know, like you're making more lye, and you see you'd have, you'd stir it longer, take longer to cool, and keep them separated. That was quite a job. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are you involved in any church activities?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not at the present time. I just didn't want to get involved in things that, if I want to go, I want to go. And so I joined up with these different things that I don't have to attend if I don't want to. I didn't want to be involved in anything. I had that too many years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you were younger, were you involved in church activities?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Basically community activities?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: All the time I had was washing and ironing and scrubbing and cooking. And I was busy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you enjoy that sort of thing? Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And just have to do the work on the routine every day, and every day, you know, well, this has to be done, this has to be done, and just go right on from one thing to another to keep that work done. I mean, you know, there's always, you know, some special stuff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What modern convenience have you enjoyed the most? What modern convenience have you enjoyed the most that you just had when you were growing up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't really know. I believe the washing machine. Bought the first washing machine in, uh, it was Maytag. Oh, see, Belmar was about a year and a half old, or 20, 27, I guess we bought it. It was a 26 model. And it had an engine on it, you know, and we had no electricity up there. But it saved a lot. Heat the water in the wash boilers, then run it, put it in the machine and wash. And other than that, we used to have a washing machine that was a wooden tub, and you had a wheel you would turn, or just had a stick up that would, and you'd stand and you'd put your foot on a stirrup, I guess you'd call it, down underneath, and that revolved your clothes around and washed them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is this the only sewing machine you've ever owned? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, really, that's the only one I own, because the other sewing machines were house mothers. And we bought this...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This was just a pedal one, right? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, and after our house and everything we had burned up in 1950, and there'd be my done, so then comes in and I thought, well, all I want a sewing machine for is just to do mending and such if that happens, so bought this second-hand sewing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's really a pretty machine.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It sews good. An old, old-timer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you watch TV very much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of evenings, quite a lot. Oh, sometimes in the daytime.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What type of shows do you watch?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, usually I like the animal shows, and I like Lawrence Wilkes and a lot of those shows.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think about the police stories and detective stories, things like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, a little bit of them is all right, you know, very educational, but as far as that shooting and all that, I don't care about it. You read nothing about that in the papers.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What magazines and newspapers do you subscribe to?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I got this Modern Life, and I got Prevention, and the Reader's Digest, and Modern Maturity, and used to take the Idaho Farmer and I. Of course, you can only read so much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you read a lot?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it just kind of depends. Sometimes I do, and then sometimes I don't read so much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When your husband was living, what were the most common things that he ever asked you about?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you like decisions about the farm and mortgages and buying more land? Who made those decisions?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, he usually always did. He'd speak about what he's had. Oh, I have a good mind to do this or a good mind to do that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But it was mostly his decision?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Usually. Well, he kind of knew what he could do and what he couldn't do. Sometimes your dad didn't agree with him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever disagree with him on big decisions? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had a pretty good tackle of it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have any advice for people who are looking for a job?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know. I think when a man, a farmer, or a man that's home all the time, they follow along from day to day. They know the money situation all comes to them, so they figure out how they can do it and what they can't do, and the living for the family and so on and so forth.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anything else that you would like to tell me?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, that's about all the stories I know, except maybe a little short story of something or other.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think we've pretty much covered most of the questions on here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's been interesting.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, it's been interesting for me. I've really learned a lot, and I'm, you know, now, well, I'm from Georgia. Oh! I'm interested in learning a little bit about the state, but talking to people develops my interest more, and we're ready to go out and read a history book on Idaho now than I was before.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, that is true. When a person, like down in Oregon, and this was my husband's folks down there and all, well, you see, it's more interesting to find out more things and so on and so forth than what they did, because they came there in an early day to Oregon, and they had a covered wagon. Both were house people, grandparents. They come from North Carolina.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anything about your life that you've changed?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't know. The past, too much. Of course, living alone, well, you've got to make different adjustments.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are some of the adjustments that you've made since your husband died?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't know, just living alone. Eating habits, used to cook quite a bit. Ha, ha, ha, ha. And first one thing, another. I don't know, just feel free to come and go as you please. And it's different. When you have a companion to go with all the time, and then, you know, then you're just alone. Of course, I companion with quite a few ladies. We have nice times together.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are there many people here that you've grown up with?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. In fact, there's no one around here that I grew up with. Now, people I know is people I met since I've been grown.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anyone around in mind?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: George Yales. The rest of the people that's come there, you know, in later years. Now, George Yales, though, he's the oldest resident there at Emida. And he, they came there, and he was a boy, and then they was away for a while, and when they came back, he grew up there and went to school there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you like life better now than when you were growing up? I mean, just kind of the way life is?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't know. I just kind of accept that this comes along.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think about the modern conveniences that you think have come about?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think they're great. I think it's nice to have them. But on the other hand, I will say that now you take some of the, now, not damning the girls, but I'm going to say if some of the younger ones had some of the other work to do, they'd have an awful time, like the old washboards. They'd have an awful time. But I think that if some of them did have more work to do at home, that I think it would help them quite a lot for their home life. Because, you see, they have everything convenient and the way to go. The husband will work and all he wants is a car and away they go. Now, there's a few of them that are good. There's some. But there's them few that just, by estimation, could be settled down more. And they'd find plenty of work right to home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think, what do you think women's roles should be?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Huh?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think women's roles should be? Or do you make a distinction?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know. I think, well, of course they have all different ideas and different things. For some reason, I like the professional ladies with their professional jobs and so on and so forth. Of course, you see, they have different, live different than what I do. Or people in, I'm going to say, different classes. Because we do know we do have different classes of people. And I think the ladies are more so than the men.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever consider working other than having children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I never had to. We had enough to get by and I had plenty of work to do right to home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you help raise the garden?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no, I didn't build myself with it. But I used to go out and hoe some. And like, hey, now they'd be away with the baler, the thrasher or something. And I'd take the kids and we'd go out and we'd chalk hay or something like that. I didn't have to. It just do it to help out. And then you see when they come back with their machine. Why then they'd come back and they'd get higher help to do those things. But a lot of times I had a big field of hay shop when they got back. You know, with the machine, this home every night. But when they get back with the machinery.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you kept a garden?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. I've planted a garden here one year since I've been here. That'd be the other side of the garage, just a small space there. And the dogs came in and said, Oh, God's sake, they just, I don't know, it seemed like they just tear up everything. And I never even got, pulled a carrot. Well, the dogs went in there and crapped around on everything. I didn't try it no more.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you make any, if there were some young women who were considering moving out to the country or say to a small town like St. Mary's, would you have any advice to give them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't know what I would. They wouldn't think. They are buggy. No, they don't seem to. Well, even the younger boys. Now, Jake up there, now they could have a nice garden up there if they'd only plant, they've got plenty of room and all. And, but, they don't. And now on the other hand, of course, the kids, as I say, there was always a working anyway, first one place and another. Time they was old enough to work and earn a little money.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you feel about your granddaughters working as opposed to staying home and raising children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know. That's their choice. Now, Judy, the one in Texas, why, she's had a babysitter with that youngster. And now to me, if a mother will stay home and take care of their little kids, I think it's far better. And I think they're closer. Because, you see, you take a little kid, you dump him. Mother goes to work. She comes back, picks her little kid up. She's tired from her work anyway. And the little kid's been away all day. Well, little kids, when they first get home after they've been away, well, they're little, you know, they're anxious to get home. Well, then there's a tired mother there with that little youngster. And they're just not with the kids enough.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever been to Texas?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever had a desire to travel around the United States?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I've kind of thought about it. I like to go, but I don't want to go alone.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there any particular place where you'd go?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, not in particular, no. Now, I have a sister living out in Redmond, Oregon, and her and another lady took off, and they took that tour of the Pacific. And she's a doctor, and she's had open-heart surgeries. And not too good, but the docs told her she could take a trip and be gone for a couple of weeks. And so they went on her and the slaves. This lady's traveled all over Europe and South America and the United States. She's a Russian. And she's traveled every place. I like her real well. I met her down there. And so they took this trip, and they were gone 16 days. And the sis got back while she had to see the doctor. I think she was in the hospital a couple of days after she got back to get straightened out better. She'd had 16 or 17 open-heart surgeries. They made a fab dub up on the big surgery. And then they sent her back to Boston, Massachusetts twice to make corrections. And a nurse would go with her and her daughter, and the arrangements all made, get on the plane, and then away she'd fly back there with her daughter and the nurse with her. And then they'd meet her there, and then she'd go to this hospital where they take care of people where there's all other doctors give up in one sense of the word. She said they had 1,000 rooms there in that place. It's a big, big place. And so they flew her back there twice. Doctors from down at Bend, Oregon.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What type of wintertime activities did you participate in when you were growing up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we used to sleigh ride. We used to go out on the ice.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Skate? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And, oh, they'd buy different games out of the snow, make fox and geese trails, and make dog and deer trails, and different things like that when they'd go out, romp around in the snow, throw snowballs at one another.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your children do those same sorts of things?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They did quite a bit the same. Well, see, we were out in the country a little ways, and other kids used to like to come there to our place and play. This is Mr. Asbury that lives here in town. He used to come there, and he'd stay there with the boys quite a lot. Robert Johnson, he lives over at Coeur d'Alene. He's married now, about their age. He used to come there quite a bit and stay. And Ralph's brother's boy used to stay there with us a lot. They lived down in Emida at the time, and their boy about our boy's age. No, we had kids around there all the time. But I don't know. Our kids stayed home, and then other kids come there because, well, it would not go down around Emida. There's nothing down there for the kids anyway. So the kids would come up there. They had nice times together. Or they'd make candy, and they'd pull taffy and maybe popcorn and eat apples. They seemed to enjoy it. Go out and play in the snow.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you make the taffy for them to pull, or did they make it themselves?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, sometimes they made it, and sometimes I made it. It worked out better if I made it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know. I've never been to a taffy pull. It just sounds really neat. I've always thought that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no. When I was a youngster, they used to have the parties, and used to have the taffy pulling. They'd make their pan of, a mother makes a pan of taffy and then stir it until it gets certain, until you start pulling it, and then give each kid so much. So you'd take it and roll it on a table of flour, and then they'd cut this, this, yarn, this, yarn, this, yarn, this, yarn, and then the kids would take it and pull it until it turned white. Oh, we used to have a lot of fun.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are some of the other things you did that are kind of like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, then they'd play different games in the house.
